x: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35. Part II (5–11) is citizenship, Part IV (36–51) DPSP and Part V the Union.
t: Link Fundamental Rights to Part III.

x: B is incorrect: Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically only when an Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression, not armed rebellion or 'internal disturbance'. After the 44th Amendment, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359.
t: Check the grounds that trigger Article 358.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right because it guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court to enforce the other rights.
t: Ask whether R states what makes A a right.

x: Equality – Articles 14–18; against Exploitation – 23–24; Freedom of Religion – 25–28; Constitutional Remedies – 32.
t: Recall the Article blocks of Part III.

x: I and II are correct: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are for citizens only, and the others (14, 20–28) extend to foreigners. III is wrong: the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property from Part III; Article 300A makes it only a legal right.
t: Separate a constitutional right from a Fundamental Right.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are available only to citizens.
II. Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25–28 are available to both citizens and foreigners.
III. Right to Property continues to be a Fundamental Right under Article 300-A.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Both are true and R explains A: High Courts' writ power under Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose', while the Supreme Court under Article 32 acts only for Fundamental Rights — so the High Courts' scope is wider.
t: Compare the scope of Articles 32 and 226.

x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 by requiring the procedure to be fair, just and reasonable (due process). A.K. Gopalan (1950) read it narrowly; Golaknath and Minerva Mills dealt with amending power.
t: Link the widening of Article 21 to Maneka Gandhi.

x: Both are true: the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights, and Article 24 bans employing children below 14 in factories and hazardous work.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Three: Habeas Corpus – 'to have the body', Mandamus – 'we command', Quo Warranto – 'by what authority'. Quashing a lower court's order is Certiorari, not Prohibition, which stops pending proceedings.
t: Separate Certiorari (quash) from Prohibition (stop).

x: Main source – US Bill of Rights; first demand – Swaraj Bill, 1895; Motilal Nehru Report – 1928; Karachi Session – 1931.
t: Order the demands for rights by year.

x: All five: the Right to Equality (Articles 14–18) covers equality before law, non-discrimination, equal opportunity in employment, abolition of untouchability and abolition of titles.
t: Recall the five Articles of the Right to Equality.

x: All three are correct: the Right to Freedom is Articles 19–22, and Article 19 gives freedoms of speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession.
t: Recall the six freedoms of Article 19.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: R names only one of the protections in A (life and liberty); it does not account for protection on conviction and against arrest.
t: A part of a list does not explain the whole list.

x: Both are true: the Right against Exploitation (Article 23) prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour.
t: Recall what Article 23 prohibits.

x: Both are true: Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise and propagate religion.
t: Recall the contents of Article 25.

x: Article 29 protects minorities' language, script and culture, Article 30 lets minorities establish and administer educational institutions, Article 32 is the Right to Constitutional Remedies and Article 23 bans trafficking and forced labour.
t: Separate the Articles, the purpose and the two parts of Article 30.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Article 29
(b) Article 30
(c) Article 32
(d) Article 23

List-II
(i) Protection of the language, script and culture of minorities
(ii) Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
(iii) Right to Constitutional Remedies
(iv) Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour

x: Dr. Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. The other options are case names, not persons who described it.
t: Link the phrase 'heart and soul' to Ambedkar.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Fundamental Rights are enforceable against the State, and Article 12 defines which bodies count as the 'State'.
t: Ask whether R defines the party in A.

x: Both are true: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning courts can enforce them, unlike the Directive Principles.
t: Contrast justiciable rights with non-justiciable DPSP.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but not the basic structure.
t: Check whether R is the source of the limit in A.

x: A.K. Gopalan – 1950, narrow Article 21; Golaknath – 1967, Fundamental Rights not amendable; Kesavananda Bharati – 1973, amendable but not the basic structure; Indra Sawhney – 1992, reservation under Article 16.
t: Order the cases by year and match the holding.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, making education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6–14.
t: Ask whether R is how Article 21A came into being.

x: Both are true: the judiciary — the Supreme Court and the High Courts — is the guardian of Fundamental Rights.
t: Recall who protects the rights.

x: Both are true: the Constitution originally had seven Fundamental Rights; removing the Right to Property (44th Amendment, 1978) left six.
t: Seven minus property equals six.

x: C is incorrect: the Right to Constitutional Remedies is Article 32 alone; Articles 29–30 are cultural and educational rights. Part III (12–35), exploitation (23–24) and equality (14–18) are stated correctly.
t: Check the Article range of each right.

x: Both are true: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are for citizens only, and the remaining Fundamental Rights are available to citizens and foreigners alike.
t: Recall the five citizen-only Articles.

x: I and II are correct (Article 21A – education; Article 24 – child labour). III is wrong: freedom to manage religious affairs is Article 26; Article 27 is freedom from taxes for promoting any religion.
t: Separate Articles 26 and 27.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 21-A provides the Right to Education.
II. Article 24 prohibits employment of children in factories and similar establishments.
III. Article 27 provides freedom to manage religious affairs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Article 14 – equality before law; 17 – abolition of untouchability; 23 – traffic in human beings and forced labour; 28 – freedom from religious instruction in certain institutions.
t: Match each Article to its right.

x: Three: the 44th Amendment (1978) deleted the Right to Property, the 86th (2002) added the Right to Education and the 97th (2011) added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c). Statement 4 wrongly gives the RTE to the 44th Amendment.
t: Pair each change with its amendment.

x: Article 15 – prohibition of discrimination; 16 – equal opportunity in public employment; 18 – abolition of titles; 14 – equality before law.
t: Recall Articles 14–18 in order.

x: All three are correct: the Right to Freedom covers Articles 19, 20, 21 and 22 — four Articles — and Article 19 gives six freedoms.
t: Count the Articles from 19 to 22.

x: 19(1)(a) – speech and expression; 19(1)(b) – assembly; 19(1)(g) – profession, occupation, trade and business; 19(1)(f) – originally property (deleted in 1978).
t: Remember (f) was property and is now deleted.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Right to Freedom of Religion has four Articles because it spans Articles 25 to 28.
t: Count the Articles in the range.

x: Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion. Managing religious affairs is Article 26, freedom from religious taxes 27 and from religious instruction 28.
t: Recall Articles 25–28 in order.

x: Both are true: Cultural and Educational Rights are two Articles — 29 protects minorities' interests and 30 gives them the right to set up and run educational institutions.
t: Separate Article 29 from Article 30.

x: Article 20 – protection on conviction; 21 – life and personal liberty; 22 – against arrest and detention; 19 – six freedoms.
t: Recall Articles 19–22 in order.

x: Three: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus and Prohibition are writs (with Certiorari and Quo Warranto). Articles 21 and 25 are rights, not writs.
t: Remove the Article numbers and count the writs.

x: Both are true: Certiorari and Quo Warranto are among the five writs, with Habeas Corpus, Mandamus and Prohibition.
t: Recall the five writs.

x: Part III is called the Magna Carta of India because it guarantees basic civil liberties against the State. "Instrument of Instructions" describes the Directive Principles, and Fundamental Duties act as a code for citizens.
t: Link each part of the Constitution to its well-known description.
s: Part III of the Constitution, containing the Fundamental Rights, is rightly described as the:

x: Both are true: Article 19(2) lists eight grounds for restricting speech, and Article 19(3) allows restrictions on assembly for sovereignty and integrity of India and public order.
t: Remember speech has the most grounds of restriction.
s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Article 19 provides eight grounds of reasonable restriction for freedom of speech and expression.
Statement B: Freedom of peaceful assembly can be restricted in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India and public order.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 22 limits preventive detention without an Advisory Board's report to three months.
t: Check whether R is the source of the limit.

x: I and II are correct: under Article 359 the President can suspend enforcement of Fundamental Rights except Articles 20 and 21. III contradicts II.
t: Remember 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

x: The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226. Article 136 is special leave to appeal, not writ power. Option C reverses the order.
t: Match 'respectively' to the right order.

x: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it makes the right to a remedy itself a Fundamental Right, giving direct access to the Supreme Court.
t: Link the description to the guaranteed remedy.

x: Mandamus ('we command') orders a public authority to perform a duty it has refused or neglected. Prohibition stops a court, Quo Warranto questions a title to office, Habeas Corpus frees a detainee.
t: Link 'perform a duty' to Mandamus.

x: B is incorrect: High Courts have wider writ power, because under Article 226 they can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose'; the Supreme Court under Article 32 only for Fundamental Rights.
t: Check which court's power is wider.

x: B is incorrect: Habeas Corpus lies against both public authorities and private individuals who detain a person illegally — it is the only writ available against private persons.
t: Remember Habeas Corpus reaches private detainers.

x: B is incorrect: Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors (or private bodies without public duties). It can lie against government companies performing public functions.
t: Recall who is immune from Mandamus.

x: A is true, R is false: Prohibition is preventive — issued while proceedings are pending to stop a court exceeding jurisdiction. Quashing a final order is done by Certiorari.
t: Separate preventive Prohibition from curative Certiorari.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the literal meaning of Quo Warranto does not explain why any public-spirited person, not only an aggrieved one, may seek it.
t: Purpose of a writ does not explain who may file it.
s:
Assertion (A): Any member of the public can move a petition for Quo-Warranto.
Reason (R): Quo-Warranto literally means "by what authority or warrant".

x: Habeas Corpus – to have the body; Mandamus – we command; Prohibition – to forbid; Certiorari – to be certified or informed.
t: Translate each Latin name.

x: Habeas Corpus – public authorities and private persons; Mandamus – public officials, statutory bodies, inferior courts and tribunals; Prohibition – judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only; Quo Warranto – person holding or claiming a public office.
t: Match each writ to who it can be issued against.

x: Prohibition – while proceedings are pending; Certiorari – after an order is made; Habeas Corpus – whenever detention is illegal; Quo Warranto – against usurpation of public office.
t: Match each writ to when it operates.

x: All three are correct: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court writ power for Fundamental Rights, Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for legal rights too, and Article 32(3) lets Parliament empower other courts locally.
t: Check each clause of Articles 32 and 226.

x: Both are true: Habeas Corpus is the remedy for illegal custody, and Mandamus for a public authority's failure to perform a legal duty.
t: Match each wrong to its writ.

x: Both are false: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty, while Quo Warranto tests a person's right to hold a public office; and Quo Warranto can be filed by any citizen, without personal injury.
t: Check the purpose and the locus standi of each writ.

x: Three are correct: Habeas Corpus can lie against a private person, Mandamus against a government company doing public work, and Certiorari after an order is made. Statement 3 is wrong — Prohibition is issued while proceedings are still pending.
t: Check the timing of each writ.

x: Certiorari quashes an order already passed by a judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative body for lack or excess of jurisdiction or error of law on the record. Prohibition acts earlier, while proceedings are pending.
t: 'Quash' points to Certiorari.

x: Habeas Corpus is the only writ that lies directly against private individuals who hold someone in illegal confinement.
t: Link private detention to Habeas Corpus.

x: Under Article 226 High Courts can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose', such as ordinary legal rights — wider than the Supreme Court under Article 32.
t: Recall the phrase 'any other purpose'.

x: Mandamus lies against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function. It does not lie against the President, Governors or purely private bodies.
t: Look for the body that has a public duty.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: R describes how Prohibition works (stopping a pending case); it does not explain why it lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.
t: How a writ operates does not explain whom it targets.

x: B is incorrect: any public-spirited citizen can seek Quo Warranto without being personally aggrieved. The office must be a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution.
t: Remember Quo Warranto relaxes locus standi.

x: Both are true: the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) exercise writ jurisdiction, and the writs come from the prerogative remedies of English common law.
t: Recall the origin of the writs.

x: Habeas Corpus – illegal detention; Mandamus – non-performance of a duty; Certiorari – illegal order already passed; Quo Warranto – any public-minded citizen may file.
t: Match each writ to the wrong it remedies.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Certiorari is curative because it acts after an order is made, while Prohibition is preventive because it acts while the case is pending.
t: Ask whether timing explains curative versus preventive.

x: Mandamus does not lie against the President or a Governor. It does lie against inferior courts, tribunals, statutory corporations and government companies performing public duties.
t: Recall the heads exempt from Mandamus.

x: Both are true: Quo Warranto literally means 'by what authority' or 'by what warrant' — it asks a person to show his title to a public office.
t: Translate the Latin phrase.
